techSplit.title: Revenue by memory technology
techSplit.content:
Micron sells three technology families: DRAM (working memory for servers, PCs and phones), NAND (flash storage) and a small NOR & other line. Each has its own supply/demand cycle and pricing.

For Micron: DRAM is roughly three-quarters of revenue and carries most of the AI-driven HBM (high-bandwidth memory) upside -- the FY2025→FY2026 jump from ~$37bn to ~$133bn in total revenue is overwhelmingly a DRAM/HBM pricing and mix story, not a volume story across all products equally.

What to watch:

  • DRAM share of revenue rising as HBM mix grows
  • NAND pricing, which has historically been more oversupplied than DRAM
  • Whether a DRAM price correction (every prior up-cycle has had one) drags the blended mix down with it

segmentRevenue.title: Revenue by business unit (current structure)
segmentRevenue.content:
Micron's current four reporting segments: CMBU (Cloud Memory -- HBM and cloud/AI DRAM), CDBU (Core Data Center), MCBU (Mobile & Client) and AEBU (Automotive & Embedded). This structure took effect from FY2023/FY2024 reporting onward.

For Micron: CMBU and CDBU together are the AI/data-center exposure the market is paying up for; MCBU and AEBU are the more cyclical, commoditised legs. Micron exited the Crucial consumer retail channel in H1 FY2026 specifically to redirect limited wafer supply into CMBU/CDBU.

What to watch:

  • CMBU's share of the mix -- it is the highest-margin segment and the one most exposed to a slowdown in AI capex
  • MCBU/AEBU growth as a read on PC, phone and auto demand outside the AI story

segmentRevenueLegacy.title: Revenue by business unit (legacy structure, through FY2024)
segmentRevenueLegacy.content:
Micron's prior four segments -- CNBU (Compute & Networking), MBU (Mobile), EBU (Embedded) and SBU (Storage) -- were reported through FY2024 before the restatement into CMBU/CDBU/MCBU/AEBU.

For Micron: these do not map one-to-one onto the current units (CNBU's data-center DRAM was split across CDBU and CMBU, for example), so this chart is kept separate rather than spliced onto the current-structure chart above.

What to watch:

  • Use this only for pre-FY2023 history; compare growth rates within each naming era, not across the regime change

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Micron Technology, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Micron Technology, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Micron Technology, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Micron Technology, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Micron Technology, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Micron Technology, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Micron Technology, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Micron Technology, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Micron Technology, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Micron Technology, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
